summary_html: Agency decides to **remove a child immediately** due to **imminent danger** prior to a court order. Federal law (ASFA/IV-E) requires later **court findings** on reasonable efforts; constitutional limits (due process; search/seizure) apply.
authority_html:
- **ASFA / SSA Title IV-E (42 U.S.C. §§ 670–679c)** — reasonable-efforts findings; permanency timelines  
- **CFSR (45 CFR Part 1355)** — monitors safety & removal decision quality

primary_citations.citation_text: New York - N.Y. Soc. Serv. Law § 411 et seq. (Child Protective Services Act – reporting requirements)
New York - Family Court Act Article 10 (Abuse/Neglect juvenile proceedings)

New York - N.Y. Soc. Serv. Law § 422 (Statewide Central Register; for investigations commenced on or after January 1, 2022 a report is indicated only where there is a fair preponderance of the evidence that the alleged abuse or maltreatment occurred, and the burden of proof at the subject's fair hearing is on the child protective service which investigated the report)

provisions_triggered.name: Due Process / Law of the Land

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: Answering certified questions from the Second Circuit, the Court of Appeals held that a child's exposure to domestic violence does not alone establish neglect or justify removal, that neglect requires a preponderance showing of actual or imminent impairment caused by the parent's failure to exercise a minimum degree of care, and that emergency removal without a court order under Family Court Act § 1024 is permissible only where the danger is so urgent that there is no time to obtain an ex parte order.
key_cases.relevance: This is the controlling New York authority on when an agency may remove a child before obtaining a court order.
key_cases.quote: emergency removal is appropriate where the danger is so immediate, so urgent that the child's life or safety will be at risk before an ex parte order can be obtained

key_cases.case_name: Southerland v. City of New York
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit
key_cases.holding: The Second Circuit vacated summary judgment for the caseworker on the father's Fourth Amendment unlawful-search claim and the children's unlawful-seizure and procedural due process claims, holding that a Family Court order obtained on a materially misleading affidavit cannot supply the warrant equivalent and that fact disputes remained over whether emergency circumstances justified the removal.
key_cases.relevance: Whether emergency circumstances existed at the moment of removal is a fact question that defeats summary judgment where the record is disputed.
key_cases.quote: In child-abuse investigations, a Family Court order is equivalent to a search warrant for Fourth Amendment purposes

key_cases.court: Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of the State of New York, Second Department
key_cases.holding: Reaching the merits under the mootness exception and reversing, the Second Department held that a parent excluded from the home by a full stay-away order of protection in an article 10 proceeding is entitled to a prompt Family Court Act § 1028 hearing applying the imminent-risk standard, because such an order is functionally equivalent to removal of the children from his care.
key_cases.relevance: The imminent-risk standard and three-court-day hearing right apply whichever side of the door the separation is accomplished from.
key_cases.quote: it must be governed by the same legal standards as are provided for removal of a child in Family Court Act §§ 1027 and 1028

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit
key_cases.holding: The Second Circuit reversed directed verdicts for city child-welfare officials and the placement agencies and remanded for a new trial, holding that a mother and her children were deprived of their constitutionally protected right to family integrity without due process where the Bureau of Child Welfare took and then kept the children for years without her consent, without a court order, and without any hearing, and that § 1983 damages liability was for the jury.
key_cases.relevance: It is the foundational Second Circuit statement that state assumption of custody must be justified by consent, court order or genuine emergency, and cannot simply continue indefinitely.
key_cases.quote: the right of the family to remain together without the coercive interference of the awesome power of the state

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit
key_cases.holding: Reviewing the preliminary injunction against New York City's practice of removing children from mothers who had been battered, the Second Circuit held that the removals may raise serious federal constitutional questions but that antecedent, unsettled questions about the Family Court Act had to be answered first, and it therefore certified three questions to the New York Court of Appeals - on the definition of neglect, on whether witnessing domestic abuse is 'danger' or 'risk' to life or health, and on whether removal requires additional particularized evidence - retaining jurisdiction over the appeal.
key_cases.relevance: This is the federal decision that produced the certification answered in Nicholson v. Scoppetta, 3 N.Y.3d 357, and it records the Second Circuit's view that a blanket presumption in favor of removal may not fairly capture the nuances of each family situation.
key_cases.quote: We agree that in some circumstances the removals may raise serious questions of federal constitutional law. We conclude, however, that uncertain issues of state law precede our own constitutional inquiry.

A determination that the investigation did not find a fair preponderance of the evidence that the alleged abuse or maltreatment occurred (investigations commenced on or after January 1, 2022)

timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Not specified in N.Y. Soc. Serv. Law § 422(8)(a)

notice_requirements.timing: In writing, no later than 7 days after receipt of the oral report
content_required: Rights of the subject of the report

statutory_basis.citation_text: 18 NYCRR 432.2(b)(3)(ii)(f) (after seeing that the children named in the report are safe, the child protective service must notify the subjects and other persons named in the report, in writing, no later than seven days after receipt of the oral report, of the existence of the report and the subject's rights)
